item.title: Second Circuit Vacates Injunction, Clearing Genius Group for $1.2 B Capital Plan
item.description:
Second Circuit Vacates Injunction, Clearing Genius Group for $1.2 B Capital Plan

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has vacated the preliminary injunction that blocked Genius Group Limited from issuing shares, raising capital, and purchasing Bitcoin, removing the legal barrier to the company’s board‑approved $1.2 billion capital plan and dual treasury strategy.

🔍 Overview

  • Genius Group (NYSE American: GNS) is a global education group delivering AI‑powered education and acceleration solutions for the future of work.
  • The company serves over 6 million users in more than 100 countries through its Genius City model and online digital marketplace.
  • It operates a dual treasury strategy that includes a Bitcoin Treasury and an AI (AGI Infinity) Treasury alongside its core education business.

⚖️ Legal Victory

  • The Second Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction issued by the Southern District of New York on March 13, 2025.
  • The injunction, which had restricted the company from issuing shares, raising capital, and purchasing Bitcoin, is now terminated and the matter remanded for status‑quo proceedings.
  • The decision ends an 18‑month legal battle in which Genius Group argued the injunction was based on inaccurate, untrue statements intended to obstruct its corporate strategy.
  • The vacatur follows a favorable ICC arbitration award issued on April 16, 2026.

💰 Financial Impact

Item Amount (USD)
Shares returned to Genius Group 7,387,374 shares
Monetary damages awarded $6,595,180.00
Legal fees and expenses awarded $1,375,988.53
  • The total monetary award (damages plus fees) equals $7,971,168.53.
  • The company plans to retire 30.1 million shares, of which the 7.4 million returned are part of that retirement.
  • The board‑approved $1.2 billion capital plan will fund the Bitcoin Treasury and the AGI Infinity Portfolio, targeting $2 billion in total assets by FY2031.
  • Net proceeds from any legal wins will be allocated 50 % to shareholder distributions and 50 % to purchase Bitcoin for the Bitcoin Treasury.

🛠️ Treasury Strategy

  • The dual treasury strategy is intended to complement Genius Group’s education business.
  • Bitcoin purchases are a core component of the treasury, subject to forward‑looking statements about price and volatility risks.
  • The AI Treasury (AGI Infinity Portfolio) is positioned to support the company’s AI‑focused initiatives.

📈 Next Steps

  • Genius Group is petitioning the district court to confirm the ICC arbitration award under Section 9 of the Federal Arbitration Act, seeking immediate return of the 7,387,374 shares and collection of the $7,971,168.53 monetary award.
  • A RICO case against LZG International officers and insiders continues in the Southern District of Florida, seeking treble damages of over $750 million.
  • The company remains subject to forward‑looking statements and associated risks, including Bitcoin price volatility, capital availability, and regulatory developments.

#GeniusGroup #AIeducation #LegalUpdate #BitcoinTreasury #CapitalPlan

Source: U.S Court of Appeals Officially Vacates Injunction Previously Restraining Genius Group’s Business Operations

item.title: AI in education boosts homework scores but lowers exam performance
item.description:
AI in education boosts homework scores but lowers exam performance

A large-scale study tracking 27,000 students in China found that generative AI improved homework efficiency but reduced exam performance over time.

🔍 Overview

After adopting generative AI, students’ homework scores rose by 18 percent, while the time spent on each assignment fell by about 30 percent, from 64 minutes to 45 minutes on average.

⚙️ Key details

  • The study, led by David Stromberg of Stockholm University, Victor Lei and Yanhui Wu of the University of Hong Kong, tracked students aged 12 to 18 for 30 months.
  • Data included homework, monthly closed-book exams, and high-stakes entrance exams across nine subjects.
  • When students sat monthly exams without AI, their scores fell by 20 percent within six months.
  • Performance in high-stakes entrance exams also declined, with the full effect emerging over a longer period.
  • The OECD’s Digital Education Outlook 2026 reached a similar conclusion.

📊 Student usage patterns

A survey by Ipsos for the Vodafone Foundation of 7,000 students aged 12 to 17 across seven European countries revealed the following uses of AI outside school:

Use Case Percentage of Students
Getting information 56%
Having terms and concepts explained 45%
Providing complete solutions to tasks 31%
Using interactive or adaptive content 29%
Creating personalised learning plans and tracking progress 20%

🎓 Student perceptions

The HEPI/Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2026, based on 1,054 full-time undergraduates in the UK, found:

  • 49 percent believe AI has improved their student experience.
  • 59 percent said AI made no difference.
  • 21 percent felt less lonely, while 20 percent felt more lonely.

🌍 Global adoption

China requires at least eight hours of AI instruction a year. In the Gulf, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all begun integrating AI into their curricula.

💡 Why it matters

Research co-authored by Dragan Gasevic describes the potential erosion of productive cognitive effort as “metacognitive laziness.”

#AIeducation #studentperformance #generativeAI #educationresearch #OECD #studentusage

Source: Faster homework, poor exam results: What AI is doing to students’ learning

item.title: New York City Bans Classroom AI Use for Students Until High School
item.description:
New York City Bans Classroom AI Use for Students Until High School

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a new policy that will ban younger schoolchildren from using AI in classrooms. The one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, will impact about 600,000 public school students in 2-K through eighth grade.

⚙️ Key Details

The new rules introduced by NYC’s Department of Education establish strict boundaries on technology inside classrooms:

  • AI Classroom Ban: Students are kept from using AI in classrooms until they enter high school.
  • Companion Chatbots: Chatbots designed specifically for companionship and mental support are banned across all grades.
  • Grading Restrictions: Teachers are barred from using AI tools to grade assignments.
  • Device and Screen Limits: Individual screen use is banned until third grade. The department is also issuing recommended screen time limits, including a maximum of 45 minutes per day for middle schoolers.
  • Device Ban Context: These changes follow NYC’s public school system introducing a bell-to-bell ban on personal internet-enabled electronic devices, including smartphones, for the 2025-2026 school year.

🧩 Exceptions and High School Rules

High school students will only be permitted to use AI in specific instances. To support this transition, they will be offered AI literacy classes twice a year to help them “think critically” before they come to “rely on it.”

Exceptions to the ban may be granted for:

  • AI tools that help students with disabilities or multilingual students.
  • Particular purposes like computer science programs.
  • Teachers using AI for lesson planning.

🧪 Limited AI Pilot Program

A “limited AI pilot” program will also be offered at up to five classes in a “small number” of high school classrooms. This program will feature tools vetted to meet safety and data privacy standards while “keeping students as the primary thinker.” These tools feature set time limits for usage and include:

Tool Purpose
Quill English language support
Edia Math
Brisk Teaching Guiding study practice
Playlab Multi-subject support
Intel AI-Ready Schools Multi-subject support

💡 Why It Matters

NYC district leaders state that the new classroom AI moratorium is one of the most restrictive policies in the US. However, countries such as Norway, Sweden, and the Netherlands have implemented nationwide changes to address similar concerns about how technology impacts developing minds.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” Mamdani said in a statement. “The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way.”

#NYCPublicSchools #AIEducation #EdTech

Source: NYC bans AI use for students until they reach high school
